paragraphs.heading: An unread script
paragraphs.text: The Indus script, also called the Harappan script, is a body of symbols made by the Indus Valley Civilisation. Most inscriptions are very short, so it is hard to tell whether the signs were true writing, used to record the language or languages people are presumed to have spoken. Despite many attempts, no one has deciphered it. No bilingual inscription is known that could help, and the script shows no major changes over time.

paragraphs.heading: Where the signs appear
paragraphs.text: The symbols turn up mostly on stamp seals and pottery, and also on tools, weapons and plates of bronze or copper. Most of the surviving texts are seals, the marks those seals left, and graffiti scratched on pottery. The seals were small and easy to carry, most just 2–3 centimetres on each side. Signs were carved, chiselled, embossed or painted onto materials ranging from terracotta and soapstone to copper, silver and gold. None has survived on perishable materials such as papyrus, cloth, wood or bark. As of 1977, about 90% of known inscribed objects came from sites in Pakistan along the Indus and its tributaries, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

paragraphs.heading: What the signs look like
paragraphs.text: Most characters are pictures of objects, local or general, or of things from nature, though many abstract signs exist too. Some signs are built from simpler picture signs, and some appear only as parts of larger signs. A few look like tally marks and are often read as early numbers. Seals often showed animals beside the text, such as elephants, bulls, water buffaloes, rhinoceros and a mythical unicorn, perhaps to help people who could not read tell where a seal came from. Most scholars agree the script was usually read from right to left, though some texts run left to right or in boustrophedon mode.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the signs
paragraphs.text: There are over 400 main signs, too many for each one to be a phonogram, so the script is generally thought to be logo-syllabic. The exact total is unclear, because experts disagree about whether some signs are separate or just versions of one sign. In the 1970s Iravatham Mahadevan listed 419 distinct signs, while in 2015 Bryan Wells estimated around 694. Just 67 signs make up 80 percent of all use, and the most common is the jar sign.

paragraphs.heading: Rise and fading
paragraphs.text: The earliest examples are on pottery and clay seal impressions from around 2800–2600 BCE, in the Early Harappan period. Digs at Harappa show that some signs grew out of potter's marks and graffiti from the earlier Ravi phase, about 3500–2800 BCE. In the Mature Harappan period, about 2600–1900 BCE, strings of signs are common on flat, rectangular stamp seals and many other objects. At Harappa the script largely stopped when inscribed seals went out of use around 1900 BCE, but it may have lasted longer elsewhere, such as at Rangpur in Gujarat. Seals and pottery fragments bearing the script, dated to about 2200–1600 BCE, are also known from the Daimabad culture in Maharashtra.

paragraphs.heading: Clues and theories
paragraphs.text: The first published seal with these symbols was a drawing by Alexander Cunningham in 1875. By 1992 about 4,000 inscribed objects had been found, some as far away as Mesopotamia. Some scholars see a connection between the Indus signs and the Brahmi script, but this has not been proven. Others, such as Gregory Possehl, see graffiti symbols from the Iron Age in central and south India and Sri Lanka as the script living on. Linguists including Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola have argued that it was related to a Dravidian language.
